title: 2,000 wild species live in our homes with us, study finds
summary: You probably have way more housemates than you think, and most of them have at least six legs, a new study suggests. If you find them, here's why scientists say you shouldn't take them outside.

image.caption: The bold jumping spider was one of the spiders commonly found in people's homes and submitted to the Never Home Alone study, to researchers' surprise. (Catherine Scott)

blocks.text: Science·Updated
You probably have way more housemates than you think, and most of them have at least six legs, a new study suggests. If you find them, here's why scientists say you shouldn't take them outside.
Never Home Alone citizen science study uncovers ecosystems in our buildings

You probably have way more housemates than you think, and most of them have at least six legs, a new study suggests. And if you find them, scientists say there are reasons why you shouldn't put them outside.

Homes in Canada and the U.S. are inhabited not just by humans and their pets but by at least 2,000 other species, from Asian lady beetles to a huge diversity of spiders to the occasional alligator, reports the study published this week in Ecology.
Bradley Allf, the Colorado State University ecologist who led the study, said the findings showcase "the ways in which we're not so separate from nature despite the many ways we try to wall it out."
Allf said his goal was to treat the indoors like the savannah or rainforest and get a sense of what the ecosystem looks like in the relatively new but growing habitat created by humans.
There's already evidence that it's full of ecological mysteries "right under our nose that we don't know very much about."

This green anole was submitted to the Never Home Alone project from a home in Raleigh, N.C. That was among the species that lead research Bradley Allf contributed to the project. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)
How science got inside so many people's homes

Allf and his team didn't explore people's homes, as scientists had in a previous study. Instead, they launched a citizen science (also known as community science) project called Never Home Alone on the iNaturalist app. It invited ordinary people to send photos of wild species they found indoors. Those species were then identified by a team of experts.
The Great Wild Indoors – Insects Hiding in Your Home

The project received more than 23,000 photos from 3,000 people in every U.S. state and every Canadian province (though not all territories) between 1996 and 2024. Most were from homes, but some were also from offices, schools, airports and other buildings.

And while experts were able to identify more than 2,000 species, the researchers believe there were more, since nearly half the observations could only be identified as belonging to a more general grouping (such as combfoot spiders), rather than as individual species. About 52 per cent of species were observed only once.
The most common species in our homes (besides us)
The most commonly recorded species in the study did include some pests, as expected. The varied carpet beetle, which can damage carpets, furniture and clothing, was No. 4, for example.
But No. 1 was the Asian lady beetle, which came as a surprise to Allf.
"We know almost nothing about what they're doing inside," he said. "And yet, they're found in hundreds of homes across the U.S. and Canada."
(CBC)
Catherine Scott is an arachnologist from Memorial University in St. John's who co-authored the study and identified many of the spiders.
"I was surprised by the diversity of spiders found indoors," she said.

While there were lots of expected species such as cellar spiders (the long-bodied cellar spider was the fifth most common in the study) and false black widows, which spin cobwebs, the bold jumping spider was also frequently reported.
"They're big and flashy and not particularly known as a house spider," she said.
But Scott noted that the most commonly reported species aren't necessarily the most common, as people tend to notice larger, more brightly coloured things that move around more.
Allf said the fact that spiders, which are predators, are so common is evidence that indoor spaces are "a real ecosystem … where species are eating one another or where there's food webs."

This is one of the most recent observations from the Never Home Alone project. Submitted from Fort George, B.C., it's been tentatively identified as a hobo spider. Spiders were among the most common types of animals found, and there was a huge diversity. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)

But he said there are lots of questions about how creatures live and interact within that ecosystem, including cellar spiders: "How often do they eat? How do they meet other cellar spiders and reproduce?"
He hopes studies like this will begin to help answer such questions.
Why you shouldn't put them outside
Allf acknowledged that many people's gut reaction when encountering other species in their homes is to squish them or take them outside.
But in fact, for many species, the indoors is their natural habitat. They're adapted to the controlled climate and food resources and are more protected from predators there.
"If they go outside, it might be a more dangerous place for them," Allf said.
This Asian lady beetle was submitted to the project from Longeuil, Que. This was the species most commonly submitted to the project in North America. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)
He gave the example of German cockroaches, a species he said has never been found outdoors.
"I think there's probably many more species like that that we just don't know about yet."
Allf suggested that when people find an organism from another species in their home, they should consider whether it's dangerous or bothering them.
"If the answers to those questions are no, then maybe just leave it there."
Scott noted that spiders are in people's homes for a reason.
"They're doing their job eating insects," she said. "They're natural pest control and they don't want to bother you, so try to coexist."
What citizen science can do

Jeremy Kerr is a University of Ottawa ecologist who has developed and used citizen science apps extensively in his research on butterflies and bees, but wasn't involved in the Never Home Alone project.
He said he loves the name and the concept and suggested it might make people feel more connected to nature and appreciate its value.
"I think there's something to be gained by simply recognizing that nature is everywhere, and maybe by extension, it's worth being curious about it," he said.

So far, he said, this is a very small citizen science database compared with larger ones containing hundreds of thousands to billions of observations that allow researchers to answer detailed questions about species such as birds. More observations about indoor ecosystems would be valuable, he said, providing a better idea of the dominant species in different regions, for example.
In fact, the Never Home Alone project is ongoing and accepting observations from around the world.
Scott hopes the publication of this study will encourage more people to contribute.
